title: Gyrate Atrophy of the Choroid and Retina: A Masterclass
summary: Gyrate atrophy is a rare, autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme ornithine aminotransferase (OAT), leading to hyperornithinemia. It presents with progressive chorioretinal degeneration and vision loss, necessitating a multidisciplinary approach.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Gyrate atrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the OAT gene (10q26.13). The metabolic hallmark is a 10-20 fold increase in plasma ornithine levels. Deficiency in OAT prevents the conversion of ornithine to pyrroline-5-carboxylate, leading to Ornithine accumulation, which is toxic to the RPE and choriocapillaris, causing the characteristic peripheral scalloped atrophy.

sections.title: Key Clinical Features
content: Nyctalopia (Night blindness) in childhood
Progressive visual field constriction
Myopia (High, often 6-10D)
Posterior subcapsular cataracts
Macular edema (Cystoid type)
Progressive peripheral chorioretinal atrophy

rows: Bone spicule pigmentation, classic ERG findings

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Plasma amino acid chromatography (Elevated Ornithine 400-1000 µmol/L).
Step 2: Fundus Examination (Peripheral scalloped RPE atrophy progressing to macula).
Step 3: Electroretinography (ERG) (Progressive reduction in scotopic and photopic responses).
Step 4: OCT (Evaluation for secondary macular edema).
Step 5: Genetic testing (Confirmation of OAT gene mutation).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to act
content: Rapid onset of central vision loss (CME)
Rapidly progressive myopia in pediatric patients
Hyperornithinemia detected in neonatal screening
Family history of early cataract development

content.explanation: O for Ornithine buildup, A for Atrophy (scalloped), T for Treatment (Vitamin B6/Pyridoxine or Diet).

sections.title: Management & Treatment
content: Dietary Modification: Low arginine, low protein diet (Ornithine is a metabolite of Arginine).
Supplementation: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) 100-500mg/day for B6-responsive patients.
Cataract Surgery: Consider early if vision is limited, but be aware of higher risk of macular edema.
CME Management: Topical NSAIDs or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Monitoring: Annual ERG, Goldmann visual fields, and plasma amino acid levels.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Not all patients are Pyridoxine responsive; metabolic monitoring is mandatory.
Early dietary intervention significantly delays visual field loss.
The scalloped edges of the atrophy are pathognomonic—it starts mid-periphery and expands.
Maintain low plasma ornithine levels < 200 µmol/L for optimal neuroprotection.
